items.question: How are plans priced?
items.answer: Every plan is billed per user, per workspace. Starter is ₹500 monthly, or ₹425/user/month on yearly (15% off). Premium is ₹1,000 monthly, or ₹850/user/month on yearly (15% off). Enterprise starts from ₹12L per year.

items.question: Which plans include billing?
items.answer: All of them. Starter, Premium, and Enterprise are billed per user, per workspace — not one bill for the whole team.

items.question: How many people and booking pages do I get?
items.answer: Starter is 1–5 people and 1 booking page with an Indlio watermark. Premium is 2–50 people and unlimited booking pages, with no watermark. Enterprise is 50+ people and unlimited booking pages, with no watermark.

items.question: What's on Premium that Starter does not have?
items.answer: Multi-currency, multi-timezone, custom forms, the customer portal, unlimited integrations, and standard reports start on Premium. Starter includes 10 integrations, basic reports, and an Indlio watermark on the booking page. Every plan is billed per user, per workspace.

items.question: What's the difference between Premium and Enterprise?
items.answer: Premium is for one studio that shares a calendar, up to 50 people, unlimited booking pages, and the standard reports. Enterprise adds custom reports, workflows, and multi-location access, plus SSO and SAML, Salesforce and Dynamics, domain control, audit logs, a data deletion API, onboarding and implementation, and dedicated account support.

items.question: Do I need a credit card to join?
items.answer: No. The waitlist is an email. We'll contact you when Indlio Bookings is ready for the first SMEs.

items.question: Can I switch plans later?
items.answer: Yes. Start on Starter and move to Premium or Enterprise when the workspace grows.

problem.title: Booking still lives in WhatsApp, calls, and sheets.
paragraphs: Small and growing businesses in India take appointments, consults, demos, and walk-ins over WhatsApp and the phone. Calendly and Zoho Bookings are built for calendar meetings — not for how these rooms actually talk to customers.

Customers want to chat before they commit. Owners need services, staff, payments, reschedules, cancellations, walk-ins, and follow-ups in one place. The gap is a pile of threads, missed slots, and no view of the day.

posts.title: Why booking software fails SMEs
posts.excerpt: Independents outgrow spreadsheets. Teams outgrow chat. The jump to enterprise software is a training project they never asked for.
body: Most booking tools are built for enterprises or for no one in particular. The first group gets a six-week implementation. The second group gets a form that still lives in someone’s DMs.
Studios, tutors, and practices do not fail because they lack features. They fail because the product asks for a training session before the first booking.
Indlio Bookings is the other path: share a link, take classes, consults, and walk-ins, and keep the calendar in one place. Live today, not next month.

posts.title: Live today, not next month
posts.excerpt: If a client can book while they are still in the room, you keep them. That is the whole product.
body: The useful test for booking software is not the feature list. It is whether someone can send a link before the client puts their shoes on.
Walk-ins, consults, and classes belong on one calendar. Everything else is noise until that path is obvious on a phone.
We are building Indlio Bookings for that moment — a public page, a shared calendar, and a reminder that feels like a person wrote it.

posts.title: Reminders that feel human
posts.excerpt: One missed class should not turn into a no-show habit. The follow-up has to sound like the studio, not a ticket system.
body: No-shows are rarely a calendar problem. They are a habit problem. A reminder that reads like a support ticket teaches people to ignore the next one.
The copy has to be short, specific, and easy to act on. Same flow on a phone as on a laptop. Most bookings happen between sessions.
That is the standard we are designing for: reminders that cut no-shows without making the front desk sound like a robot.
